newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila official seeks to stop sugar exports to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Manila official seeks to stop sugar exports to U.S.

text.p: Philippine Sugar Regulatory Administration chief Wilson Gamboa said on Friday he had asked President Fidel Ramos to order a stop to the country's sugar exports to the United States.

"May I recommend that we formally desist complying with our U.S. export commitment at the earliest beginning sugar year 1997/1998 (Sept/Aug)," Gamboa said in a letter to Ramos on March 31, a copy of which was released to reporters on Friday.
The Philippines is a beneficiary of a U.S. sugar import programme under which it buys the commodity from developing countries at premium prices.
Gamboa said the Philippines should stop exporting sugar to the United States so Manila need not import from other countries to meet its own domestic requirements.
The Philippines incurred an average of 250,000 tonnes sugar shortfall in the past three years with sugar harvests at 1.75 million tonnes against consumption of two million tonnes, he said.
"(Sugar) shipments to the United States have become the new milking cow of a few," Gamboa said.
He said Philippine "trading producers" and traders refused to export sugar if domestic prices are higher than the U.S. export price.

"Because the Philippines cannot renege from its commitment, trading producers and traders hold government hostage by demanding that they be given premium incentive for their export- a practice so exploitative and inimical to the industry...," Gamboa said.

Philippine sugar producers were allowed by the government to import 1.25 tonnes for every tonne of sugar exported to the U.S. in the first quarter of the current crop year as incentive for filling up the country's U.S. sugar quota, he said.
A surge in cheaper sugar imports in the past months had depressed prices of local raws, Gamboa said.
"People are disturbed that we export our home-grown sugar when we import our needs," he added.
In the 1995/1996 crop year the Philippines imported some $159 million worth of sugar against export revenues of $96.602 million.
"I believe the United States shall look kindly at this proposal. Because of our domestic sugar situation, to us, this quota has long ceased to be a favour," Gamboa said.
